title: Mercy, Not Sacrifice
summary: The people call one another to return to the LORD, confident that the God who tore them will heal them and raise them up on the third day. God answers with grief: their loyalty is like morning mist, gone by midday. He desires loving devotion and the knowledge of God more than sacrifice, but Israel has broken the covenant, and even its priests are murderers on the road to Shechem.
story: At the end of chapter 5 God withdrew to his place until Israel would seek his face. Chapter 6 opens with what looks like the answer: a song of return. But God's reply in verses 4-6 shows that something is wrong. The people's words are right, but their loyalty does not last. The chapter contains one of the most important sentences in the prophets, God's desire for mercy rather than sacrifice, which Jesus quoted twice. It then returns to the indictment, naming places where violence and unfaithfulness have taken root, and closes with a brief word that a harvest of judgment is appointed for Judah too.
historical:
The chapter belongs to the same troubled period as chapter 5, the 730s BC, when Israel suffered Assyrian invasion and internal violence. The place names in verses 7-10 point to specific events that are now mostly lost to us. Gilead, east of the Jordan, was the home of the fifty men who helped Pekah assassinate King Pekahiah in Samaria (2 Kings 15:25), which may be why Hosea calls it a city of evildoers tracked with blood. The road to Shechem, an ancient city in the hill country and a city of refuge (Joshua 20:7), was apparently the scene of murders involving a band of priests.

The word Adam in verse 7 may be the town of Adam on the Jordan, where the waters of the river stood in a heap when Israel crossed into the land (Joshua 3:16). The following word there suggests a place, and some scholars think Hosea refers to a covenant-breaking event at that town, though nothing more is known of it. The BSB's like Adam reads the word as the first man, who also broke God's command. Both readings are defended.
cultural:
The images of verses 3-4 come from the farming year in Israel. Crops depended on the early rains of autumn and the late spring showers, and the prophet compares God's coming to that reliable rain. In the dry season, heavy dew overnight and morning mists water the land, but they burn off within hours. Israel's loyalty is like that: present at dawn and gone by noon.

Sacrifice was central to Israel's worship, commanded in the law as a means of fellowship with God and atonement for sin. Hosea is not abolishing it. The prophets repeatedly insist that sacrifice without faithfulness is worthless (1 Samuel 15:22; Isaiah 1:11-17; Amos 5:21-24; Micah 6:6-8). In Hebrew idiom, I desire this, not that often means I desire this more than that, as the second line shows: the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings.
literary: The chapter is built as a dialogue. Verses 1-3 are the people's words, a short song of return with the rhythm of a liturgy. Verses 4-6 are God's reply, beginning with two anguished questions: What shall I do with you, O Ephraim? What shall I do with you, O Judah? The tone is that of a parent at a loss. Verses 7-10 resume the indictment with a list of places, and verse 11, possibly linked to the start of chapter 7, turns to Judah. Watch the contrasts: the people say God will come like the rain, and God says their love is like the dew that vanishes. The same imagery of water measures the difference between God's faithfulness and theirs.

outline.t: Come, let us return to the LORD
God's reply: loyalty like morning mist; mercy, not sacrifice

doctrines.note: The people's song uses the right words but lacks lasting change, and God sees through it. True repentance is not a brief feeling but a turning that produces steady loyalty.

Israel has transgressed the covenant (verse 7). What God wants from his covenant partners is loving devotion and knowledge of him, the relationship itself, which sacrifice was meant to express, not replace.
God's questions in verse 4 show his grief. He is not indifferent to Israel's failure, and his faithfulness, as sure as the sunrise and the spring rain, stands against their fleeting loyalty.

words.note: Hesed, loyal covenant love. It appears twice: Israel's hesed is like morning mist (verse 4), and God desires hesed, not sacrifice (verse 6). The BSB renders it loyalty and mercy in these verses. The Greek translation used by the New Testament rendered it with a word meaning mercy, which is how Jesus' quotation reads in Matthew.

Daat, knowledge. God desires the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings. As in 4:1 and 4:6, it means a living relationship of trust and obedience. The people say let us press on to know the LORD, but their knowing does not last.

Qum, to arise or to raise up. On the third day He will raise us up (verse 2). In context the verb pictures a nation revived after being struck down, like a wounded person helped to stand. Whether the verse anticipates the resurrection of Christ is discussed under the hard question.

Adam, which can mean a man, humankind, the first man, or the town of Adam on the Jordan. Verse 7 has been read all three ways: like Adam (the first man who broke God's command), like men, or at Adam (a place where Israel was unfaithful). The word there in the next line gives some weight to the place reading.

christ: Jesus quoted verse 6 twice in Matthew's Gospel. When the Pharisees objected to his eating with tax collectors and sinners, he told them to go and learn what it means (Matthew 9:13). When they criticized his disciples for picking grain on the Sabbath, he said that if they had known what the verse meant, they would not have condemned the innocent (Matthew 12:7). For Jesus, Hosea's words were a key to God's heart and a rebuke to religion that keeps rules while despising people. Many Christian readers, from the early church onward, have also heard in verse 2 a pattern fulfilled in Jesus, who was raised on the third day. Paul says Christ was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:4) without naming a text, and Hosea 6:2 is one of the passages often proposed; on this reading, Jesus, as Israel's representative, experiences the revival the nation hoped for.

hard.q: Is the people's song in verses 1-3 sincere, and does the third day point to Jesus?
hard.a:
Readers divide over verses 1-3. Many interpreters read them as shallow repentance: the people assume that God will heal them quickly and automatically, as surely as the sunrise, without confessing any specific sin, and God's reply in verse 4 exposes their loyalty as short-lived. Others read them as a genuine model prayer, the very seeking God waited for in 5:15, and see God's reply as grief that even this response will not last. The text supports elements of both: the words are good, but the pattern of Israel's history makes God doubt their staying power.

The phrase after two days, on the third day is a Hebrew way of saying after a short time, and in context it speaks of Israel's national revival. Some interpreters therefore see no reference to Christ. Many Christian interpreters, noting Paul's statement that Christ was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures, think Hosea 6:2 is among the texts he had in mind, with Jesus as the one in whom Israel's hope of being raised is fulfilled. The New Testament never quotes the verse, so the connection is one of pattern rather than explicit citation.

questions: Israel's loyalty was like morning mist. What makes spiritual commitment last beyond the first moment of feeling?
Jesus used God desires mercy, not sacrifice to challenge religious people. Where might religious practice crowd out mercy in your own life or church?
The people were confident God would heal them without naming their sin. Why is honest confession necessary for real return?
